newsitem.title: USA: Wide White house group knew of Hubbell aid: Times.
newsitem.headline: Wide White house group knew of Hubbell aid: Times.

text.p: A larger number of White House officials than has been conceded knew about efforts to help associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell following his fraud conviction, the New York Times said on Thursday, citing new interviews.

The White House has acknowledged close Presidential advisers tried to find work for Hubbell after he resigned from the Justice Department to face a criminal investigation, but it said the help was not organised, the paper said.
But interviews point to a wider involvement of White House officials at different levels, the Times reported.

Hubbell resigned from the Justice Department in 1994 and was sent to jail in 1995 after he pleaded guilty to fraudulently billing clients at the Rose law firm of Little Rock, Ark., before he joined the Clinton Administration.
He and Hillary Clinton were partners at the firm.

Hubbell received more than $400,000 from various businesses and organisations after leaving the Justice Department in April 1994. Federal and Congressional investigators are examining how much President Clinton and other officials knew about payments to Hubbell, the paper said.
The Times said a dozen or so senior Clinton administration aides found themselves involved with Hubbell's situation.

At dinner with a recently retired aide in 1995, Hubbell asked the aide if Indonesia's Riady family, which had already paid Hubbell $100,000, would keep him on the payroll as he faced prison, the newspaper said.
The aide, Mark Middleton, told Hubbell to ask the Riady family directly, Middleton's lawyer was quoted as saying in the Times.
According to White House documents and Administration advisers, some aides started in 1994 to track Hubbell's legal and personal situation, the paper said.
